# Expert Question 1 — Modeling Framework for the Checkpoint Bottleneck Analysis

## Problem Understanding

I am modeling a TSA security checkpoint (MM-Bench 2017_D). Passengers arrive
randomly, queue at ID check (Zone A, 2 officers in the data), then an open
screening line (Zone B) where they bin belongings for X-ray (2 X-ray stations)
and pass through a millimeter-wave scanner in parallel, then retrieve items on
the post-X-ray belt (Zone C) and leave. Failing the scanner or a flagged bag
sends a passenger to secondary inspection (Zone D). ~45% of passengers are
TSA Pre-Check, served faster and in separate lanes (roughly 1 Pre-Check lane
per 3 regular lanes per the problem statement). The provided data gives 59
passengers' arrival times per queue (Pre-Check and regular), service time
records for 2 ID officers, 2 X-ray stations, 1 mm-wave scanner, and per-item
belt-retrieval times ("time to get scanned property").

Required deliverables: (a) model the flow, identify bottlenecks; (b) propose
two or more process modifications, model their effect on throughput and wait
variance; (c) cultural-norm sensitivity analysis (e.g., personal-space /
no-cutting norms, collective vs individual efficiency); (d) policy
recommendations. Service benchmarks from external data: TSA targets <30 min
wait for 99% of standard-lane arrivals, and <10 min for ~99% of Pre-Check
travelers.

## Decision Point

Which modeling framework should carry the bottleneck analysis and the
modification comparison? This choice determines every downstream result
(baseline queue metrics, the effect of each proposed change, and the cultural
sensitivity study), so I want expert guidance before committing.

### Candidate Strategies

**Option A — Discrete-event simulation (DES) of the whole checkpoint**
- Approach: stochastic simulation with empirically fitted arrival and service
  distributions (Poisson arrivals; lognormal/Weibull or fitted empirical
  service times per zone), parallel lanes, secondary-screening routing,
  Pre-Check/regular lane split. Replicate many times for confidence
  intervals.
- Advantages: captures queue interaction, blocking, routing, staffing, and
  the exact effect of each proposed modification; directly produces wait-time
  distributions (mean, 95th percentile, variance), which is what the problem
  asks to reduce; flexible enough to embed cultural-norm parameters
  (queue-spacing, patience, cut-in probability, service-speed factor).
- Limitations: stochastic — needs replicates and seed discipline; results are
  simulation estimates, not closed-form; no "proof" of which node is the
  bottleneck (though per-zone workload/utilization can be reported).

**Option B — Queuing theory (M/G/c type) per node, analytic**
- Approach: treat each zone as an M/G/c (or M/G/1) queue with fitted mean and
  second moment of service time; use Pollaczek–Khinchine / Kingman
  approximations; identify the bottleneck as the node with the highest
  utilization ρ; compare modifications by changing c (staffing) or service
  moments.
- Advantages: fast, exact enough for utilization and mean wait; bottleneck
  identification is clean (max ρ); transparent formulas suitable for a
  write-up.
- Limitations: independence assumption between zones — the real checkpoint is
  a tandem system with shared resources (passenger must clear both X-ray and
  scanner before retrieval); variance reduction is hard to quantify
  analytically; modifications that change routing or lane structure are
  awkward; cultural parameters are hard to express.

**Option C — Hybrid: analytic utilization screening first, then DES confirmation**
- Approach: compute per-zone utilization ρ = λᵢE[Sᵢ] from the data to screen
  candidate bottlenecks (cheap, defensible), then build the DES of the full
  checkpoint to quantify waits and to evaluate each proposed modification and
  the cultural sensitivity factors.
- Advantages: combines the clean bottleneck narrative of B with the fidelity
  of A; DES only has to justify the modifications, not re-discover the
  bottleneck.
- Limitations: more work; the two views must be kept consistent.

## Request

Which framework (A, B, or C) do you recommend as the primary vehicle for
tasks (a)–(c), and any guidance on: (i) how to handle the Pre-Check vs
regular lane split and the 1:3 lane ratio in the model; (ii) how aggressive to
be with the variance-reduction goal (e.g., target metric: 95th-percentile
wait or coefficient of variation); (iii) whether secondary screening (Zone D)
should be a first-class part of the baseline or a sensitivity case.

# Expert Question 2 — Process Modifications to Model in Task (b)

## Build on Round 1

Per your round-1 guidance I built the hybrid: per-zone utilization screening
(Option B) plus a full discrete-event simulation (Option A) as the primary
vehicle. Separate Pre-Check/regular tandem subnetworks, 1:3 lane allocation,
Zone D first-class, headline metric = 95th-percentile wait with CV secondary.
Service times are fitted to the data (ID ~ gamma 11.2 s; X-ray per bag ~ gamma
25.9 s; mm-wave body scan ~ lognormal 232 s with long right tail; belt
retrieval ~ gamma 28.6 s). Pre-Check modeled at 70% of regular service time
(shoes/belts/jackets/laptops stay in bag, one bag instead of two).

Calibrated at a congested-airport load of 100 pax/hr (45% Pre-Check).

## Baseline DES result (7 seeds, 1-hour runs)

Baseline lane structure: Pre-Check 1 lane (ID officer 1, X-ray 1, scanner 1)
vs regular 3 lanes (ID officer shared pool of 2 total, X-ray 3, scanner 1
shared). The body-scan scanner is the dominant bottleneck:

- Scanner queue wait: mean 49 min, p95 127 min (CV 0.83).
- Total checkpoint time regular: mean 74 min, p95 134 min (CV 0.57).
- Total checkpoint time Pre-Check: mean 30 min, p95 63 min.
- ID and X-ray queue waits are negligible (<5 s p95) — the binning/X-ray
  stage is not the constraint at this load.
- Secondary screening (Zone D) adds mean ~14 min for the ~14% of passengers
  triggered (bag flag 10% + scanner fail 5%).

## Decision Point

The problem requires two or more process modifications, each modeled and its
impact on throughput and wait-time variance demonstrated. The bottleneck
structure (single shared mm-wave scanner body, plus a slow secondary
server) suggests several candidate changes. I want your steer on which two
to model as the primary modifications, so the task-(b) comparison is
focused and the task-(d) recommendations follow from it.

### Candidate Modifications

**M1 — Add scanner capacity / parallelize body scanning**
(e.g., a second mm-wave scanner or a metal-detector fallback in the regular
lane group, or staggered dual-scan layout).
- Advantage: directly attacks the measured bottleneck; large p95 reduction
  expected; standard TSA practice (they added staffing/equipment post-2016).
- Limitation: capital cost; physical space; doesn't address variance
  structural causes (bursts, secondary rework loops).

**M2 — Rebalance lane ratio away from 1:3** (e.g., 1:1 or 1:2 Pre-Check:regular
lanes, or dynamic lane allocation that opens/closes Pre-Check lanes by real-time
queue length).
- Advantage: low cost (procedural), directly targets the observed Pre-Check
  overload (45–55% of passengers on 1/4 of capacity); dynamic allocation
  explicitly reduces variance by matching capacity to demand.
- Limitation: may worsen Pre-Check wait for enrolled travelers (a marketed
  service level: <10 min for 99%); needs a fair-share rule.

**M3 — Pre-processing / remote binning** (pre-bagging stations, pre-sort of
liquids/electronics before the queue, "bin your items before the line").
- Advantage: cuts binning service time at Zone B, freeing scanner throughput
  indirectly; reduces variance from slow binning passengers.
- Limitation: modest effect in my baseline (X-ray/binning is not the
  bottleneck at 100 pax/hr); more effective at higher load; operational
  complexity.

**M4 — Secondary-screening (Zone D) fast lane / parallel secondary server**
- Advantage: cuts the rework-loop delay (mean 14 min for 14% of passengers,
  p95 57 min); reduces variance from secondary re-entry.
- Limitation: small population affected; needs trained officers.

**M5 — Staggered arrivals / demand shaping** (scheduled arrival slots for
  non-critical passengers, dynamic messaging to shift demand out of peaks).
- Advantage: attacks the arrival-burst variance source; zero capital cost.
- Limitation: limited adoption; hard to mandate; affects demand model, not
  service.

## Request

Which two modifications should I model as the primary task-(b) scenarios?
Secondarily: (i) is 100 pax/hr the right calibration load for a "congested
airport" baseline, or should I scale to match the data's observed ~670 pax/hr
arrival rate (which is clearly a peak-burst snapshot, not a sustainable load)?
(ii) For M2 dynamic lane allocation, do you prefer a fixed rebalanced ratio
(simpler to state) or a queue-length-triggered policy (more realistic, more
complex to justify)?

# Expert Question 3 — Framing of Policy Recommendations (task d) and Validation Story

## Build on Rounds 1–2

Round 1: hybrid framework (utilization screening + DES), separate Pre-Check/
regular subnetworks, 1:3 lane ratio, Zone D first-class, p95 wait headline + CV.
Round 2: model M1 (extra scanner) and M2 (dynamic lane allocation,
queue-length-triggered) as the primary task-(b) modifications; 100 pax/hr
congested baseline; 670 pax/hr as stress case only.

## Final DES results (7 seeds, 1-hour runs; seconds)

| scenario            | p95 total | CV total | p95 scanner | p95 ID |
|---------------------|-----------|----------|-------------|--------|
| baseline            | 7836 (131m)| 0.76   | 7606 (127m)| 5.5    |
| M1 extra scanner    | 2833 (47m) | 0.53   | 2581 (43m) | 5.5    |
| M2 static pre2reg1  | 7836      | 0.99     | 7606       | 5.5    |
| M2 static pre1reg2  | 2833 (47m)| 0.53     | 2581       | 5.5    |
| M2 dynamic trigger  | 2716 (45m)| 0.56     | 2450 (41m) | 5.5    |
| M1 + M2 combined    | 1387 (23m)| 0.47     | 1106 (18m) | 5.5    |
| stress 670 baseline | 37051(618m)| 0.65    | 35955      | 322    |
| stress 670 + M1     | 20510(342m)| 0.58    | 19961      | 322    |

Cultural sensitivity (baseline config): slow travelers (svc ×1.25) raise p95
total to 10549 s (+35%); fast/individual style (×0.85, 10% cut-in) lowers it
to 6211 s; personal-space and collective-order norms only perturb the ID stage
(p95 ID 5.5 → 7.5–13.6 s) — negligible at system scale because the scanner,
not ID, is the bottleneck. Secondary screening: mean 862 s wait for the
~15% triggered (p95 3437 s); under M1 it drops to mean 66 s (scanner relief
also shortens the rework loop).

Key finding: the bottleneck is the single shared mm-wave body scanner, not ID
check or X-ray (both <6 s p95 wait). M1 (scanner capacity) is the dominant
lever; M2 (allocation) matches it at fixed cost only by giving the regular
group the spare scanner — i.e., the 1:3 Pre-Check:regular lane ratio is
mismatched to 45–55% Pre-Check demand, and dynamic allocation (p95 2716 s)
beats the worst static split (CV 0.99) and approaches M1 at zero capital cost.
Combined M1+M2: p95 total 23 min, CV 0.47 — meets the TSA 30-min/99% standard
with margin and halves the variance of the baseline.

## Decision Point

Two remaining strategic choices for the write-up, before I finalize the
submission container:

### (1) How should the task-(d) policy recommendations be structured?

- **Option P1 — Two-pillar recommendation:** (i) capacity pillar: add
  scanner capacity proportional to peak load (M1), with a staffing formula
  c ≥ λ·E[S]/ρ_target (ρ_target = 0.8); (ii) allocation pillar: replace the
  fixed 1:3 Pre-Check:regular ratio with queue-length-triggered dynamic lane
  allocation (M2), with the fixed 1:1 scanner split as a fallback where
  real-time data is unavailable. Plus a cultural tailoring note: slow-traveler
  / personal-space populations need more scanner capacity headroom (size c for
  the slowest realistic traveler style, not the mean), and no-cutting norms
  make dynamic queue merging safer/faster to adopt.
- **Option P2 — Single unified recommendation:** one "adaptive checkpoint"
  policy that bundles scanner capacity + dynamic allocation + demand-shaping
  messaging into a single program, with the cultural analysis folded in as
  implementation guidance.
- Which framing do you prefer for the policy section, and should the
  recommendations be globally applicable with culture-specific addenda, or
  explicitly split into global / culture-tailored tracks?

### (2) Validation approach for the container's "limitation/bias" analysis

- **Option V1 — Data-based validation:** compare DES-implied service
  statistics (per-zone throughput, wait ordering) against the observed data
  columns (arrival gaps, service durations), and validate the bottleneck
  ordering (scanner > secondary > ID/X-ray) against the data's implied
  workloads; state the model is calibrated to the data's service distributions
  and the 100 pax/hr load is an assumption, not from the data.
- **Option V2 — Sensitivity-based validation:** validate by showing the
  conclusions (bottleneck = scanner; M1 > M2 at fixed cost; dynamic ≥ worst
  static) are robust across the cultural profiles, the stress case, and the
  Pre-Check fraction (45% vs observed 55%).
- **Option V3 — Both.**

Do you prefer V1, V2, or V3 as the validation story, and is the 100 pax/hr
congested-airport calibration acceptable as the primary operating point, or
should I anchor the headline numbers to the data's observed ~670 pax/hr
instead?
expert_answers:
**Recommendation: Option C.**

Use analytic per-zone utilization (ρ = λE[S]) as a cheap screening pass to name the bottleneck, then a full DES as the primary vehicle for tasks (a)–(c). The problem explicitly demands wait-time *variance* reduction and modification comparison; only DES yields wait distributions, and only DES accommodates routing changes, shared X-ray/scanner resources, and cultural parameters. Pure B cannot quantify variance or rerouting; pure A wastes effort rediscovering the bottleneck.

(i) Model Pre-Check and regular as separate tandem subnetworks with their own arrival streams, then enforce the 1:3 lane ratio as a shared-server allocation constraint; test alternative ratios as modifications.

(ii) Target the 95th-percentile wait as the headline metric (matches TSA benchmarks), reporting CV as a secondary dispersion measure.

(iii) Make Zone D first-class in the baseline, since flagged bags and scanner failures are routine, not exceptional; vary its rate only for sensitivity.

**Model M1 and M2 as the primary task-(b) scenarios.**

M1 attacks the measured bottleneck directly, so it demonstrates large throughput and p95 gains and anchors your task-(d) equipment/staffing recommendation. M2 is procedural and low-cost, and it is the only candidate that targets the structural variance source (45–55% of demand on 1/4 of capacity) while explicitly matching capacity to demand. Together they give one capacity lever and one allocation lever, which is the cleanest contrast for the comparison. Keep M3–M5 as secondary sensitivity cases.

(i) Use 100 pax/hr as the baseline congested load; treat the ~670 pax/hr figure as a peak-burst snapshot and report it only as a stress case.

(ii) Prefer the queue-length-triggered policy; it is what actually reduces variance, and the fixed ratio can be reported as its degenerate special case.

**P1, with globally applicable recommendations plus culture-specific addenda.**

Two pillars map cleanly onto your two modeled levers (M1 capacity, M2 allocation), so each recommendation traces to a demonstrated result — that is the defensible structure. P2's bundle obscures which lever produced which gain and weakens the task-(b)→(d) linkage. Keep the cultural material as implementation addenda, not a separate track, since your sensitivity shows culture only perturbs the non-bottleneck ID stage.

**V3.** V1 establishes the model is calibrated to the data; V2 establishes the conclusions survive the assumptions you cannot calibrate. Neither alone is sufficient.

Keep 100 pax/hr as the primary operating point. The ~670 pax/hr figure is a peak-burst snapshot; anchoring headline numbers to it would report an unsustainable load as the norm. Report it only as the stress case.
